\begin{CRchronicle}{96}
On the tenth day of Ash, the dark month’s first Account-day, Sella Vail carried the basket down before first light at the half-pace she keeps from every open slate and set it in the moot-post’s shade. Two hundred people leaned toward the block; eight pigs came over the boards, uncounted aloud. Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner. His hands were large and clean. He wiped his thumb twice on his apron before he touched nothing, passed a finger over the figure, and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says}, sending it twice over the basket. “The levy is called. It is not called by me,” he said, and spoke of \emph{your house}, never I; then something low to the block about kindness being entered, and the block answered nothing. He went off with the box locked and Ash’s first subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. Seven arithmetics now stand behind one printed figure, and seven are seven and not one account.

Hessa Rale took the slate up the road before noon, her hand to it before her eyes to the crowd, the writing to her sleeve. To a woman who asked what she carried she said, “I don’t read it. I carry it.” The bell went four, four and a gap; nobody crossed himself. Below the north bridge the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set for an uncalled measure, the market selling over him as water over a stone. At the pot board a silent woman turned a cup a quarter and set it back; at the market’s edge a shape in cast-offs caught light on a green sliver. Each was a seventh with no eighth, and neither was named.

On the eleventh and twelfth the house kept its ordinary days. Ilva drew at the well with the pail against her knee; to a woman asking what the reading had taken she answered, “Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account,” her hand toward her sleeve and staying, the notches unread. Tarn kept six where the house could check and the seventh at the lip, and said \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late, keeping the late because it puts off the paying. Jorra Vail spoke to the wheel before any person and put his bent finger into the cold damper ahead of a sentence unfinished.

At each going of the light Sella lifted the twice-mended pot with her thumb first where the wire crossed the crack and left the hairline showing. The figure read was still not the figure paid; no signature stood on the space. The hand came up an inch toward the river’s note, took a small intake, held it whole and let it go on the same low note, and two hundred and fifty-eight honest answers stand, each an object and not a power.
\end{CRchronicle}
